lesson.title: Before You Trust the Chi-Square Table
lesson.summary: Three conditions, random, independent, and large counts, must hold before a chi-square statistic's P-value can be trusted, and the large counts check depends on expected, not observed, counts.
lesson.body:
A chi-square statistic is only as trustworthy as the conditions behind it. Before you compute a P-value from any chi-square procedure, whether goodness-of-fit, homogeneity, or independence, three conditions need to hold.

Random: the data must come from a random sample or a randomized experiment. Without randomness, there is no valid basis for treating the observed counts as representative of anything beyond the specific individuals studied, and the whole idea of a sampling distribution stops making sense.

Independent: individual observations must be independent of one another, meaning knowing one individual's category tells you nothing about another individual's category. When sampling without replacement from a finite population, check the 10% condition: the sample size should be no more than 10% of the population size, so that removing sampled individuals does not meaningfully change the probabilities for those still available.

Large counts: every expected count, not observed count, must be at least 5. This condition is easy to state but easy to misread, since it is the values you compute, the counts you would predict under the claim, or from the row and column totals of a table, that must be checked, not the raw data you collected. The reason this condition exists is technical but important: the chi-square distribution is a smooth, continuous curve used to approximate the true, lumpy sampling distribution of the discrete X squared statistic, and that approximation is only accurate when the expected counts are reasonably large. When an expected count is tiny, say 1 or 2, the true sampling distribution is badly skewed and the smooth chi-square curve gives a misleading P-value.

Check this against the candy example from the previous chapter: the expected counts were 30, 20, 20, 10, 10, 10, all comfortably at least 5, so the large counts condition is satisfied there. Now imagine the same claimed percentages applied to a much smaller bag of only 20 candies. The expected counts would become 20 times each proportion: 6 brown, 4 yellow, 4 red, 2 orange, 2 green, 2 blue, which still sum to 20. Three of those expected counts, orange, green, and blue, are below 5, so the large counts condition would fail, and a standard chi-square test should not be trusted on that smaller bag without first combining some categories, for instance lumping orange, green, and blue into a single other category, to push the expected counts back up to 5 or more.
